title: Control systems
tagline: Mathematical modelling of mechanical, electrical and thermal plants, transfer functions and block diagrams, time and frequency response, stability, root locus, PID design, state-space methods and digital control
summary: Control systems is the design of feedback: how to make a machine follow a command it was not built to follow and reject the disturbances it was not built to reject. The course develops the modelling of plants by impedance reflection and linearisation, the transfer-function and block-diagram algebra, the time and frequency response of loops, the stability criteria and the fundamental trade-offs of feedback, root-locus and frequency-domain design, the practical PID controller and its tuning, state-space design with observers, and the changes wrought by implementing the controller in a computer.
overview: Every plant in this curriculum - every motor, furnace, column, robot arm, suspension and aircraft - is unstable, sluggish or inaccurate on its own, and every one of them can be made well behaved by measuring the output, comparing it with what is wanted, and doing something about the difference. That is the whole of feedback control, and the whole of this course is the question of how much you may do, and how you may know that you have not done too much.

The first third of the course is modelling and representation. A plant is described by a differential equation; the Laplace transform converts that equation into a rational function of $s$; the transfer function lets a mechanism of several physical kinds - an electrical amplifier driving a hydraulic valve driving a mechanical load - be drawn as a diagram of blocks and reduced by algebra that is nothing but the distributive law. Poles, zeros, the pole-zero map and the impulse response are then the vocabulary, and the second-order system is the grammar: one number, the damping ratio, fixes overshoot, rise time, settling time and the resonant peak, and the reason a control engineer thinks in second-order terms is that most closed loops are made to look second-order on purpose. Stability enters as the location of the closed-loop poles, and the Routh-Hurwitz criterion decides the question from the coefficients of the characteristic polynomial without ever solving for them.

The middle of the course is the two great design methods, and they are the same method seen from two sides. **The root-locus method** draws the closed-loop poles as a function of gain and lets you place a dominant pair by putting a zero where it bends the locus through the region you want; it is geometric, it is exact for the system you drew, and it tells you the price of every choice. **The frequency-response method** - Bode plots, gain and phase margin, the Nyquist plot and the $M_s$ circle - is what you use when you do not know the model, because it is the method designed for a measured response; and its central result, Bode's integral and the water-bed theorem, is the most important sentence in the subject: the sensitivity integrated round the loop is fixed by the plant's unstable poles, so a sensitivity peak pushed down in one band must rise somewhere else. **Gain margin and phase margin are not luxuries; they are the reason a controller that works in simulation works on the plant, and the reason a design with a $6 \mathrm{dB}$ margin and a $15^{\circ}$ margin, though it will meet every specification on paper, will be returned.**

The last third is the subject as it is actually practised. **PID control** is the observation that three terms - proportional, integral and derivative - will control almost anything, that the tuning rules of Ziegler and Nichols of 1943 are still the starting point in a commissioning shop, and that the difference between a textbook PID and a working one is anti-windup, derivative filtering, split ranging and a bumpless transfer. **State-space control** drops the single-input single-output restriction, puts the system in first-order form, and delivers controllability, observability, pole placement, the observer and the separation principle - and with them the sobering realisation that a state estimator is a model, and that a bad model in the feedback path is worse than no model at all. **Digital control** then inserts the sampler and the zero-order hold, converts $s$ to $z$, and shows that a sample rate chosen too generously costs nothing and a sample rate chosen too meanly costs the loop: the rule of thumb is that the sample frequency must exceed twenty times the gain-crossover frequency, and the reason is that the hold's phase lag is $\omega T / 2$ radians at the frequency where you are trying to have margin. **The course ends where every control engineer's day begins: with a plant you cannot model exactly, a sensor you cannot place where you want, an actuator that saturates, and a specification that says how much of all three you may live with.**
outcomes: Derive the transfer function of a mechanical, electrical, thermal or fluid plant from its governing equations, draw the physical system as a block diagram and reduce it by the rules of block algebra, and identify the load and the sensor loading in a real measurement chain
Obtain the impulse, step and frequency response of a system from its poles and zeros, and predict the shape of a response from a pole-zero map without solving a differential equation

Derive the complete time response of the standard second-order system, compute rise time, peak time, percentage overshoot, settling time and the steady-state error to step, ramp and parabolic inputs, and use the error constants $K_p$, $K_v$ and $K_a$
Apply the Routh-Hurwitz criterion to a characteristic polynomial, find the range of a parameter for stability, and explain what the criterion cannot tell you about relative stability

Construct a root locus by the standard rules, design a lead, lag or lead-lag compensator by pole-zero placement, and evaluate the design against both the transient specification and the sensitivity to plant variation

Sketch and interpret Bode, Nyquist and Nichols plots for a real plant including a transport delay, compute gain margin, phase margin and the $M_s$ peak, and use the gain-crossover frequency as a direct statement of closed-loop bandwidth

Apply the Nyquist criterion and the principle of the argument to a loop with an unstable pole or a delay, and explain the water-bed constraint imposed by Bode's sensitivity integral on any achievable loop shape

Design, tune and implement a PID controller: choose between the interacting and non-interacting forms, apply Ziegler-Nichols and lambda tuning as starting points, and handle integral windup, derivative kick, actuator saturation, and manual-to-automatic transfer

Write a linear system in state-space form, test it for controllability and observability, place the closed-loop poles by state feedback, build a full-order observer, and apply the separation principle to combine the two

Discretise a continuous plant and controller by the zero-order hold and by Tustin's transformation, choose a sampling rate from the gain-crossover frequency, and analyse the closed-loop discrete system in the $z$-plane including the deadbeat and the root-locus designs

chapters.title: Modelling of dynamic systems
chapters.summary: Impedance and reflected impedance through gears and levers, linearisation about an operating point, and the mechanical, electrical, fluid and thermal analogies.

chapters.title: Transfer functions and block diagrams
chapters.summary: Laplace-transform models, poles and zeros, algebra of block diagrams, signal-flow graphs and Mason's rule.

chapters.title: Time response
chapters.summary: First- and second-order step responses, identification from a test, steady-state error and the error constants.

chapters.title: Feedback and stability
chapters.summary: Loop gain, sensitivity, the characteristic equation, the Routh criterion and the cost of feedback.

chapters.title: Root locus
chapters.summary: Construction rules, breakaway and asymptotes, gain from the magnitude condition, and lead and lag design by pole placement.

chapters.title: Frequency response
chapters.summary: Bode and Nyquist plots, gain and phase margins, the sensitivity peak and the waterbed integral.

chapters.title: PID control
chapters.summary: The ideal and practical forms, anti-windup and derivative action, and tuning by Ziegler-Nichols, by pole placement and by frequency response.

chapters.title: State-space design
chapters.summary: Controllability, pole placement, state observers, integral action and the LQR trade-off.

chapters.title: Digital control
chapters.summary: Sampling, the z-transform, aliasing and the hold, discrete pole placement and the deadbeat and PID implementations.

history.title: Watt's flyball governor, and the machine that watches itself
history.detail: James Watt did not invent the centrifugal governor — conical-pendulum regulators were used in seventeenth-century clocks and centrifugal regulators in eighteenth-century windmills — but in 1788 he adapted one to the rotative steam engine and made it the symbol of the machine that regulates itself. Two flyballs on hinged arms lift a sleeve as the shaft speeds up, the sleeve closes the throttle, and the engine settles at a speed that falls slightly as the load rises — the proportional 'droop' of the first widely used feedback controller. **It is an elegant device and not always a stable one: later governors were known to hunt, and Maxwell's 1868 analysis was written to explain why. His conclusion — that the stability of such a system depends on the roots of a polynomial, and that the governor and engine together give an equation of third order that can have unstable roots — is the moment control began to change from a craft of adjusting linkages into a branch of differential equations.**

history.title: Maxwell on governors, and Routh on polynomials
history.detail: Maxwell's 'On governors', published in the Proceedings of the Royal Society in 1868, showed that the stability of a governed engine is a question about the roots of a polynomial with real coefficients, and gave the conditions for the low-order cases he could handle. Edward John Routh, the celebrated Cambridge mathematics coach, gave the general algebraic answer — a test that decides whether all the roots have negative real parts without finding them — in his Adams Prize essay *A Treatise on the Stability of a Given State of Motion* (1877), and Adolf Hurwitz reached an equivalent determinant form independently in 1895; the Routh–Hurwitz criterion is the oldest result in this course that engineers still use routinely. **The criterion is a good test of a student's understanding of what a stability analysis is for: it does not tell you how stable a system is, only whether a polynomial has a root in the right half-plane, and a design that passes it with roots barely inside the left half-plane will still ring badly on the test bed.**

history.title: Black's amplifier and Nyquist's plot
history.detail: Harold Stephen Black, a Bell Telephone Laboratories engineer, conceived the negative-feedback amplifier on 2 August 1927 while crossing the Hudson on the Lackawanna ferry to work, sketching it on a page of his newspaper; the patent, filed in 1928, was granted only in 1937, and feedback amplifiers became standard in long-distance telephone repeaters. Harry Nyquist, in 'Regeneration theory' in the Bell System Technical Journal of 1932, turned the same loop into a diagram — the plot of the open-loop frequency response — and gave the rule by which the encirclements of the point $(-1, 0)$ tell you whether the closed loop is stable. **The two together are a founding act of modern control: the discovery that feedback buys accuracy and linearity at the price of stability, and the discovery of a test for the price. That the theory was worked out on amplifiers carrying telephone conversations explains why the frequency-response method still speaks the language of the communications engineer.**

history.title: Ziegler and Nichols, and the tuning rule that will not die
history.detail: John Gregory Ziegler and Nathaniel Marston Nichols of the Taylor Instrument Companies published 'Optimum settings for automatic controllers' in the Transactions of the ASME in 1942. Their ultimate-gain method — put the controller in proportional-only mode, find the gain at which the loop oscillates steadily, and set the working gain and the reset and rate times as fixed fractions of that gain and of the oscillation period — together with a companion method based on the open-loop step response, was a piece of applied engineering of the first rank: it aims at a quarter-decay response, which is fast but has a poor margin. **It is still among the first things a commissioning engineer tries, and it is one reason so many installed controllers ring. Many later tuning rules — Cohen–Coon, Chien–Hrones–Reswick, lambda tuning, the Internal Model Control settings, and the relay auto-tuners — can be read as corrections to Ziegler–Nichols that trade some speed for robustness.**

history.title: Bode, and the shape of a loop
history.detail: Hendrik Wade Bode published *Network Analysis and Feedback Amplifier Design* in 1945, having spent years at Bell Labs turning the frequency-response method into a design discipline: the asymptotic magnitude-and-phase plot that carries his name, the phase- and gain-margin ideas, the relation between the slope of the magnitude curve and the phase of a minimum-phase system, and the sensitivity integral, which says that for a stable open loop the logarithm of the closed-loop sensitivity integrates to zero over all frequencies (Freudenberg and Looze extended it in 1985 to plants with unstable poles, which make the integral positive). **Bode's integral is a reason control theory is not merely a set of techniques. It says that disturbance rejection is conserved: push the sensitivity below one in one band and it must rise above one in another, and the area of the rise does not depend on how clever the controller is. Every claim of a controller that rejects every disturbance is measured against that sentence.**

history.title: Evans, and the root locus
history.detail: Walter R. Evans, teaching servomechanisms and working on guidance and control problems at North American Aviation, published 'Graphical analysis of control systems' in the Transactions of the AIEE in 1948 and 'Control system synthesis by root locus method' in 1950, and gave the industry a way to see where the closed-loop poles go as a gain is turned: the locus of the roots of $1 + K G H = 0$, drawn from the angle condition, with the gain read off from distances. His Spirule, a transparent protractor with a pivoting arm, made the construction quick by hand. **The method spread quickly through industry and universities because it makes the effect of adding a zero visible. A compensator is a pole and a zero, and on a root-locus plot you can see the locus bend towards the zero and away from the pole, which is the art of lead and lag compensation; and the method survived the arrival of digital computation because a designer choosing where to put a zero wants to see the trade, not just be told the answer.**

history.title: Ragazzini, and the control loop that samples
history.detail: John Ralph Ragazzini, with Lotfi Zadeh — the same Zadeh who would later invent fuzzy sets — introduced the $z$-transform to sampled-data control in 1952, and Ragazzini and Gene Franklin's book *Sampled-Data Control Systems* of 1958 set out the theory that let a computer sit inside a control loop: the $z$-transform of a plant preceded by a sampler and followed by a zero-order hold, the mapping $z = e^{sT}$, and the design of digital controllers by transform methods. **The practical content of that work includes a rule of thumb that has survived every later improvement in hardware: the sample rate must be high enough that the hold's phase lag at the gain crossover, about $\omega T / 2$ radians, is a small fraction of the phase margin you intend to have. A loop with $50^{\circ}$ of margin sampled at only ten times its crossover frequency loses $18^{\circ}$ — more than a third of its margin — before the controller does anything at all.**

history.title: Kalman, and the state of the system
history.detail: Rudolf Emil Kalman, then at the Research Institute for Advanced Studies in Baltimore, published 'On the general theory of control systems' and 'A new approach to linear filtering and prediction problems' in 1960, and with them moved the subject from the frequency domain to the time domain, from the single input to the vector, and from the transfer function to the matrices $A$ and $B$. Controllability, observability, state feedback, the observer and — with Richard Bucy in 1961 — the continuous-time optimal estimator all follow; and in the early 1960s Stanley Schmidt's group at NASA Ames adapted the filter to the navigation problem of the Apollo programme. **The intellectual gain is that a controller with an observer is revealed as a model of the plant running in parallel with it, which makes the model's accuracy a limit of the design and explains why a state-feedback controller designed on a nominal model can be more fragile than a PID. The engineering gain is that the same machinery handles a system with twelve states and three inputs, for which single-loop frequency-domain methods have no clean answer.**
